title: An account from the public registration form widens the workspace's TOTP window and lockouts, then guesses into a TOTP-protected administrator

steps.action: call users.listByStatus with roles=admin as the newly registered ordinary account
steps.result: every administrator's username and email address, which is both the target list and the login identifier the next step needs

steps.action: post statistics.telemetry batches of updateCounter events naming Accounts_TwoFactorAuthentication_MaxDelta and Block_Multiple_Failed_Logins_Attempts_Until_Block_By_Ip
steps.result: a TOTP acceptance window of 4001 time steps, so one random six-digit code in about 125 verifies, and a per-address failed-login ceiling of 1550 instead of the shipped 50

steps.action: guess six-digit codes at POST /api/v1/login naming the victim by email address, which isValidAttemptByUser never counts because it reads the username as typed
steps.result: 525 guesses, none refused by any lockout, and then a session token for the administrator

combined_impact: Proven in the lab: an account created through the shipped public registration form held a full administrator session three minutes later. It read a private, administrator-only setting (HTTP 200) that the same attacker's own account is refused (HTTP 403). Attacker capability before: an ordinary user with the default role, holding the victim's password but stopped by TOTP. After: the victim's administrator session, with the second factor reduced to a formality for the whole workspace while the window stays raised, and no account lockout ever engaging. The blast radius during the window is every account on the workspace, not just the one attacked, because both settings are workspace-wide; the run restored them.
preconditions: An account from the public registration form (the shipped default), and the victim's password: phished, reused or breached, which is the exact situation a second factor exists to survive. No administrator action and no non-default setting are needed; the chain changes two settings itself and the run puts both back.
fix_order: Fix step 2: close the set of settings ids updateCounter will touch (updateStatsCounter.ts, VULN-057), so a telemetry handler cannot write a security setting. One change breaks the chain, because step 2 is what removes both brakes: at the shipped window of 1 a blind guess lands once in 333,000 and at the shipped ceiling of 50 the address is blocked long before that. Side effect: keeps telemetry and removes only the weakness: the handful of counters the first-party client reports keep working and any other id is refused, which no shipped client sends. The per-account lockout bug (VULN-032) should be fixed too, by keying the failure counter on the resolved account rather than on the identifier as typed; on its own that fix leaves the widened window exploitable from many source addresses.
